revealWordProblem.title: Apply: School District Size
revealWordProblem.text: A large school district has 621,000 students in grades kindergarten through 12. The district currently has 1 teacher for every 20 students but plans to hire more teachers to have 1 teacher for every 15 students. How many teachers does the school district need to hire to reach its goal?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The district hires 10,350 teachers. It currently has 621,000 ÷ 20 = 31,050 teachers, and it needs 621,000 ÷ 15 = 41,400 teachers to reach the new ratio. The difference is 41,400 − 31,050 = 10,350 teachers to hire.

turnAndTalk.question: The station must divide 1,344 nutrition bars equally among 12 crew sections. Before dividing, about how many bars should each section get, and how do you know?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Estimating with friendly numbers checks whether the quotient is reasonable.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students estimate using 1,200 ÷ 12 = 100 (or similar) to predict roughly 100+ bars per section, identifying 1,344 as the dividend and 12 as the divisor.

turnAndTalk.question: You used partial quotients for 1,344 ÷ 12. What steps did you use, and how do they build to the final quotient?

turnAndTalk.extend: Why does it not matter whether you start with 12 × 100 or 12 × 50 in partial quotients? Will you reach the same quotient?

turnAndTalk.question: The station's observation deck seats 2,160 visitors equally across 18 viewing sections. How does multi-digit division tell each section's seat count, and how can you check it?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Dividing 2,160 by 18 gives each section's seats; multiply back to check.
turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students compute 2,160 ÷ 18 = 120 and verify with 18 × 120 = 2,160, explaining the quotient is the per-section seat count.
turnAndTalk.extend: If the deck held 2,170 visitors instead, what would the quotient and remainder be, and what would the remainder mean in this situation?
extendStems: With 2,170 visitors the quotient is ___ and the remainder is ___.

turnAndTalk.question: In a division problem, what is the difference between the quotient and the remainder, and what does each one tell you?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The quotient is the size of each equal share; the remainder is what is left over.

stems.en: The quotient tells me ___, and the remainder tells me ___.
stems.es: El cociente me dice ___, y el residuo me dice ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain the quotient is the number in each group while the remainder is the amount left that cannot be shared equally, and a remainder of 0 means it divides evenly.
turnAndTalk.extend: When is it correct to round a quotient UP because of a remainder, and when should you drop the remainder? Give an example of each.
extendStems: I round up when ___, for example ___.
I drop the remainder when ___, for example ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Divide Multi-Digit Numbers, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, then add up how many you took out to get the quotient.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy tied to 6.NOS.2 — not just "I multiplied." They should connect steps to the key idea.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who made the common mistake from today's lesson? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.

visual.title: Breaking 1,344 ÷ 12 with partial quotients
visual.caption: 100 + 12 = 112, so each of the 12 sections gets 112 bars

conceptIntro.heading: How do you divide big numbers?
conceptIntro.intro: Dividing means splitting a total into equal groups. Partial quotients let you divide a big number by taking away easy chunks until nothing is left.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, then add up how many you took out to get the quotient.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I want 1,344 ÷ 12. The dividend is 1,344 and the divisor is 12.
First I take a big easy chunk: 12 × 100 = 1,200. I subtract: 1,344 − 1,200 = 144.
Now I divide 144: 12 × 12 = 144. I subtract: 144 − 144 = 0, so nothing is left.
I check by multiplying: 12 × 112 = 1,344. Correct, and the remainder is 0.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's do 384 ÷ 8. What easy chunk of 8 can we take from 384? (8 × 40 = 320.)

youDo.title: Now it's your turn
lines: Next, you will sort the steps that solve 1,344 ÷ 12 and then divide on your own.
Remember: take away easy chunks, then add how many you used.

explore.instructions: Break apart the division 1,344 ÷ 12 using partial quotients. Sort each partial product — does it help build toward the answer, or is it NOT a step in this division?

discourse.prompt: How do partial quotients help you divide large numbers? What is 1,344 ÷ 12?
discourse.sentenceFrame: 1,344 ÷ 12 = ___ because I can break it into 12 × ___ = 1,200 and 12 × ___ = 144, then add the partial quotients.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
The digits look familiar, but the place value is off: 12 × 480 = 5,760. Check where each digit of your quotient lands.
12 × 380 = 4,560, which misses 4,896. Recheck the very first step: how many 12s fit into 48?
hints: Division asks how many groups of 12 fit inside 4,896, so the answer should be in the hundreds, not the tens.
Work through the long division one place value at a time, and remember to write a 0 in the quotient whenever the divisor does not fit.
Start with 48 ÷ 12 = 4, so the hundreds digit is 4. Now bring down the 9 — how many 12s fit into 9? Decide that digit and keep going.
hintsEs: La división pregunta cuántos grupos de 12 caben dentro de 4,896, así que la respuesta debe estar en las centenas, no en las decenas.
Haz la división larga un valor posicional a la vez, y recuerda escribir un 0 en el cociente cuando el divisor no quepa.
Empieza con 48 ÷ 12 = 4, así que el dígito de las centenas es 4. Ahora baja el 9: ¿cuántos 12 caben en 9? Decide ese dígito y continúa.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
That is ten times too large: 25 × 2,890 = 72,250. Count the place values in your quotient.
25 × 389 = 9,725, which overshoots 7,225. Recheck the tens digit after you take out the first 200 groups of 25.
hints: Think in 25s: this asks how many groups of 25 make up 7,225, and that count will be in the hundreds.
Pull out friendly chunks instead of guessing — 25 × 100 = 2,500 is an easy piece to subtract.
Two hundred 25s make 5,000, and 7,225 − 5,000 = 2,225 is still left. Keep pulling 25s out of 2,225 to finish the count.
hintsEs: Piensa en grupos de 25: esto pregunta cuántos grupos de 25 forman 7,225, y esa cantidad estará en las centenas.
Saca bloques fáciles en vez de adivinar: 25 × 100 = 2,500 es una parte sencilla de restar.
Doscientos grupos de 25 dan 5,000, y todavía quedan 7,225 − 5,000 = 2,225. Sigue sacando grupos de 25 de 2,225 para terminar el conteo.

optional.stem: A school orders 3,648 pencils packed 24 to a box. How many boxes are there?
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
24 × 160 = 3,840, more pencils than the school ordered. Trim the tens digit and multiply back to test it.
24 × 144 = 3,456, which leaves 192 pencils with no box. Those still need boxes, so the quotient is not finished.
optional.stemEs: Una escuela pide 3,648 lápices empacados de 24 por caja. ¿Cuántas cajas hay?
hints: Every box holds the same number of pencils, so this is asking how many equal groups of 24 fit into 3,648.
Divide 3,648 by 24 by taking out easy chunks first, like 24 × 100.
24 × 100 = 2,400, and 3,648 − 2,400 = 1,248 pencils are still unboxed. How many more 24s fit into 1,248?
hintsEs: Cada caja tiene la misma cantidad de lápices, así que esto pregunta cuántos grupos iguales de 24 caben en 3,648.
Divide 3,648 entre 24 sacando primero bloques fáciles, como 24 × 100.
24 × 100 = 2,400, y quedan 3,648 − 2,400 = 1,248 lápices sin empacar. ¿Cuántos grupos de 24 más caben en 1,248?

optional.explanation: 31 × 164 = 5,084 exactly, so there is no remainder.
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
31 × 174 = 5,394, which is past 5,084. Your estimate for the tens digit is one too high — multiply back to test it.
Your quotient is doing the right work, but check the leftover. Multiply the quotient by 31 and subtract from 5,084 to see whether anything actually remains.
optional.explanationEs: 31 × 164 = 5,084 exactamente, así que no hay residuo.
hints: You are finding how many groups of 31 fit inside 5,084 — and whether anything is left over at the end.
Estimate first: 31 is close to 30, and 5,084 ÷ 30 is a little under 170. Then divide exactly.
31 × 100 = 3,100, so 5,084 − 3,100 = 1,984 is still left. Keep taking 31s out of 1,984 and watch whether anything remains.
hintsEs: Estás buscando cuántos grupos de 31 caben dentro de 5,084, y si sobra algo al final.
Estima primero: 31 está cerca de 30, y 5,084 ÷ 30 es un poco menos de 170. Luego divide con exactitud.
31 × 100 = 3,100, así que todavía quedan 5,084 − 3,100 = 1,984. Sigue sacando grupos de 31 de 1,984 y observa si sobra algo.

optional.stem: Path 1: The first arcade door shows 4,928 ÷ 7. Which quotient lights the correct path?
optional.explanation: 7 × 704 = 4,928 exactly, so the quotient is 704 with no remainder.
choiceFeedback: Check your division steps—try a smaller or larger chunk first.
The digits are close, but 7 × 740 = 5,180. Check where the 0 belongs in the quotient — its position changes the value a lot.
A remainder can never be as large as the divisor. If your leftover is 7 or more, another whole group of 7 still fits, so keep dividing.
optional.stemEs: Camino 1: La primera puerta del arcade muestra 4,928 ÷ 7. ¿Cuál cociente ilumina el camino correcto?
optional.explanationEs: 7 × 704 = 4,928 exactamente, así que el cociente es 704 sin residuo.
hints: Behind the arcade story this is plain division: how many groups of 7 are inside 4,928?
Divide place by place, and write a 0 in the quotient at any spot where 7 does not fit.
49 ÷ 7 = 7, so the hundreds digit is 7. Next you look at 2 — does 7 fit into 2? Record that digit and keep going.
hintsEs: Detrás de la historia del arcade esto es una división normal: ¿cuántos grupos de 7 hay dentro de 4,928?
Divide valor posicional por valor posicional, y escribe un 0 en el cociente en cualquier lugar donde el 7 no quepa.
49 ÷ 7 = 7, así que el dígito de las centenas es 7. Después miras el 2: ¿cabe el 7 en 2? Anota ese dígito y continúa.

optional.stem: Path 2: A side corridor displays 6,045 ÷ 9. Which door is correct?
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
Check by multiplying: 9 × 672 = 6,048, which is already more than 6,045, so this quotient is too big before any remainder is added.
Your remainder makes sense, but a digit went missing from the quotient. Count place values — 6,045 reaches the thousands, so the quotient reaches the hundreds.
optional.stemEs: Camino 2: Un pasillo lateral muestra 6,045 ÷ 9. ¿Cuál puerta es la correcta?
hints: The divisor does not have to fit evenly here, so your answer may include a remainder.
Divide one place value at a time and keep careful track of what is left after the very last step.
60 ÷ 9 = 6 with 6 left over, so 6 goes in the hundreds place. Bring down the 4 to make 64 and keep going, watching the final leftover.
hintsEs: Aquí el divisor no tiene que caber exactamente, así que tu respuesta puede incluir un residuo.
Divide un valor posicional a la vez y lleva bien la cuenta de lo que queda después del último paso.
60 ÷ 9 = 6 y sobran 6, así que el 6 va en las centenas. Baja el 4 para formar 64 y continúa, atento a lo que sobra al final.

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Repair the machine for 3,724 ÷ 7. Label the parts: dividend = 3,724, divisor = 7.

optional.correctWork: After Step 2 there are still 14 left, and 7 × 2 = 14, so 14 − 14 = 0. The machine stopped one chunk early. The true quotient is 500 + 30 + 2 = 532 with remainder 0. The check confirms it: 7 × 532 = 3,724, which equals the dividend.
hints: After subtracting 210 you have 14 left. Can the divisor 7 still divide into 14? How many times?
7 × 2 = 14, so add one more partial quotient. The repaired check should give 7 × quotient = 3,724, the original dividend.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
12 × 68 = 816, which lands short of 936. Check the tens digit of your quotient before you bring down the next number.
That is close: 12 × 76 = 912, which is 24 away from 936. Multiply your quotient back by 12 each time to see whether it lands exactly on the dividend.
hints: Estimate first: 12 × 70 = 840 and 12 × 80 = 960, so the quotient must land between 70 and 80.
Use partial quotients: subtract an easy chunk like 12 × 70 from 936, then see how many 12s fit in what's left.
Compute 936 − 840 = 96. Now ask: how many 12s make 96? Add that count to the 70 you already took out.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
A zero slipped into the tens place: 5 × 507 = 2,535, which is more than 2,485. Recheck what is left after you divide the hundreds.
You are very close, but 5 × 496 = 2,480 and 5 are still left over. A leftover that big means the ones digit is not finished yet.
hints: Size it up: 5 × 500 = 2,500, just a bit more than 2,485 — so the quotient is a little under 500.
Break 2,485 into friendly pieces that 5 divides easily, like 2,000 + 450 + 35, and divide each piece by 5.
Start with 2,000 ÷ 5 = 400. Then divide 450 by 5 and 35 by 5, and add all three partial answers together.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
9 × 94 = 846, which overshoots 756. Recheck the tens digit by asking how many 9s fit into 75.
9 × 86 = 774, a little past 756. Nudge the ones digit down and multiply back to test it.
hints: Anchor on a fact you know: 9 × 80 = 720, which is close to 756 — so the quotient is just above 80.
Use partial quotients: take out the chunk 9 × 80 first, then divide whatever is left over by 9.
Compute 756 − 720 = 36, then ask how many 9s make 36. Add that count to the 80 you already used.

approaching.label: Use partial quotients to divide. Fill in the blanks.
hints: Read the row left to right: each chunk is a friendly multiple of the divisor, and the quotient is the SUM of the chunk sizes.
After each chunk, subtract to find what remains, then choose a second chunk that finishes the leftover exactly.
Row 1: try the chunk 8 × 40. Subtract that product from 384, then count how many 8s fit the leftover. The quotient is 40 plus that count.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
9 × 135 = 1,215, which is past 1,125. Recheck the tens digit by asking how many 9s fit into 22.
So close: 9 × 124 = 1,116, and another 9 still fits. Multiply back every time to see whether you land exactly on the dividend.
hints: Notice that 1,125 splits nicely into 900 + 225 — and both of those pieces are multiples of 9.
Divide each friendly piece by 9 separately, then add the two partial quotients together.
Start with 900 ÷ 9 = 100. Now divide 225 by 9 (it helps to see 225 as 180 + 45) and add your two results.

approaching.title: Spot the Mistake in 1,134 ÷ 9

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Divide 1,134 ÷ 9 using partial quotients. Dividend = 1,134, divisor = 9.

approaching.correctWork: The student stopped one chunk early. After Step 2 there are still 54 left, and 9 × 6 = 54, so 54 − 54 = 0. That last partial quotient of 6 must be added: 100 + 20 + 6 = 126. Check: 9 × 126 = 1,134, which equals the dividend.
hints: After Step 2 the student still has 54 left. Can 9 divide into 54? How many times?
9 × 6 = 54, so add one more partial quotient. The repaired quotient checks as 9 × 126 = 1,134.

onLevel.label: Complete each division problem.
hints: Every quotient can be checked by multiplying back: quotient × divisor should rebuild the original number exactly.
Use partial quotients: pull out easy multiples like 100 times or 10 times the divisor first, then divide what's left.
For 672 ÷ 8: take out 8 × 80 = 640, leaving 32. How many 8s fit in 32? Add that to 80, then use the same plan on each row.

onLevel.label: Match each division problem to its quotient.
hints: Estimation narrows the matches fast: round each dividend and divisor, then see which quotient card is the right size.
You can also work backwards: multiply a quotient card by the divisor and check whether it rebuilds the dividend.
Try 450 ÷ 18: since 18 × 20 = 360 and 18 × 30 = 540, the quotient sits in the twenties. Find the card in that range and verify it.

onLevel.stem: A warehouse has 2,184 items to pack into boxes of 14. How many boxes are needed?
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
14 × 166 = 2,324, which is more items than the warehouse actually has. Check the tens digit of your quotient.
14 × 155 = 2,170, which leaves 14 items with no box. Multiply back to test whether your quotient uses up every item.
hints: The question asks how many groups of 14 fit into 2,184 — that phrase 'how many boxes' signals division.
Estimate to anchor yourself: 14 × 150 = 2,100 is close to 2,184. Then use partial quotients to finish.
Take out 14 × 150 = 2,100 and subtract: 2,184 − 2,100 = 84. How many 14s make 84? Add that count to 150.
onLevel.stemEs: Un almacén tiene 2,184 artículos para empacar en cajas de 14. ¿Cuántas cajas se necesitan?

onLevel.instructions: Sort each division problem: does it divide evenly (no remainder), or does it have a remainder?
hints: Each card shows the finished division — scan for the letter 'R', which flags a leftover remainder.
You can also verify a card: multiply quotient × divisor; if it rebuilds the dividend exactly, the division is even.
Check '144 ÷ 12 = 12': 12 × 12 = 144 with nothing left over, so that card goes in Divides Evenly. Verify the others the same way.

onLevel.title: Spot the Mistake in 2,058 ÷ 14

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Divide 2,058 ÷ 14 using partial quotients. Dividend = 2,058, divisor = 14.

onLevel.correctWork: Step 3 picks a chunk that is too big: only 98 remained, but 14 × 8 = 112 is larger than 98 — you cannot subtract more than what is left. Use the largest chunk that still fits: 14 × 7 = 98, so 98 − 98 = 0. The quotient is 100 + 40 + 7 = 147 with remainder 0. Check: 14 × 147 = 2,058, which equals the dividend.
hints: Look at Step 3: only 98 remained after Step 2. Can you really subtract 112 from 98? A negative remainder means the chunk you picked is too big.
Try the largest chunk that still fits: 14 × 7 = 98 leaves 98 − 98 = 0. So the quotient is 147 with no remainder, and 14 × 147 = 2,058.

extending.title: Find Sonia's Mistake
extending.correctWork: After subtracting 80, Sonia has 16 left. 16 ÷ 16 = 1, so she needs one more partial quotient. The correct answer is 90 + 5 + 1 = 96.
hints: After Step 4, Sonia has 16 remaining. Is she really done dividing?
16 ÷ 16 = 1. She stopped too early — she needs to add that last partial quotient.

extending.prompt: The station must load 3,360 ration packs equally into 14 storage pods. Show how to solve this using partial quotients. Explain each step and check your answer by multiplying.
extending.sentenceFrame: 3,360 ÷ 14 = ___. First I used 14 × ___ = ___, then 14 × ___ = ___. The partial quotients add to ___. I checked by multiplying: 14 × ___ = 3,360.
hints: Re-read the sentence frame: it wants partial quotients — big friendly chunks of 14 subtracted one step at a time.
Start with a large chunk like 14 × 200, subtract it, then keep taking smaller chunks until nothing is left.
First chunk: 14 × 200 = 2,800. Subtract: 3,360 − 2,800 = 560. Now find how many 14s fit in 560 and add all your chunk sizes.

extending.label: Solve each problem using long division. Show the quotient and any remainder.
hints: Each row asks for TWO things: the whole-number quotient AND whatever is left over — and a remainder can be 0.
Run the long-division cycle — divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — until no digits remain; the last leftover is the remainder.
For 2,578 ÷ 13: begin with 25 ÷ 13 → 1, subtract 13, bring down the 7. Keep cycling and record whatever remains at the very end.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Divide Multi-Digit Numbers is skipping a placeholder zero in the quotient when a digit doesn't divide evenly, which shifts every digit after it out of place. For example, dividing 3,216 ÷ 3: 3 ÷ 3 = 1, but the next digit 2 doesn't divide by 3, so a 0 must be written before continuing — bring down the 1 to make 21 ÷ 3 = 7, then bring down 6 ÷ 3 = 2, giving the correct quotient 1,072. A student who skips writing that 0 and jumps straight to 21 ÷ 3 = 7 ends up with 172 instead of 1,072 — an answer off by a factor of ten. Always check: does a digit in your quotient go missing every time you 'can't divide'? If so, you dropped a placeholder zero.
